name: Sauber-Mercedes C9
hook: Le Mans timed it at 400 km/h down the Mulsanne straight, and the next year the organisers cut that straight in half with two chicanes.
story:
Peter Sauber trained as an electrician, then sold cars in a small Swiss town called Hinwil. In 1970 he built a racing car in the basement of his parents' house in Zurich. He called it the C1, after his wife Christiane. He drove it himself and won the Swiss sports car championship that year.

Mercedes-Benz had walked away from top-level racing in 1955 and stayed away. When it came back, in the late 1980s, it did not build its own car. It went to Sauber. The 1988 cars ran in black, with the electronics brand AEG down the flanks. They won. So for 1989 the board decided: paint them silver.

That is the C9. Silver, barely a sponsor on it, a three-pointed star on the nose. It lost one race all season, at Dijon. At Le Mans it came home first, second and fifth. A man who started in a basement had brought the Silver Arrows back.
description: The C9 was a Group C prototype built by Sauber, a small Swiss team based in Hinwil, around a twin-turbocharged five-litre Mercedes-Benz V8. It raced from 1987 and was the car that carried Mercedes-Benz back to the front of sports car racing after three decades away. In 1989 it ran in plain silver, won the World Sportscar Championship, and took first, second and fifth at the Le Mans 24 Hours. Its successor was badged a Mercedes-Benz outright.
